On the road to El Junco, the familiar seascapes of the Galápagos give way to green hillsides. The lagoon lies in the highlands of San Cristóbal, inside the crater of an extinct volcano. Rainwater fills its freshwater basin, which is ringed by dense vegetation. After the beaches and black coastal lava, it is fascinating to discover this other side of the island.

Visitors come to walk and watch birds. Frigatebirds appear over the water, using the freshwater lagoon to bathe. Their slender silhouettes, long wings and swift turns over the surface quickly catch the eye. Spend a little time at the crater rim and you can watch the clouds move across the sky and the reflections shift on the water.

The name El Junco comes from the junco plant that grows in this area. The damp greenery and gentle outlines of the slopes are especially noticeable along the trail. The crater's low edges offer a view of the entire lagoon, while changeable weather gives the scenery a succession of colours. Comfortable footwear and light rain protection are useful for the visit.

El Junco makes a natural addition to an exploration of inland San Cristóbal. After time at sea, the pace slows here: walk down towards the water, watch the birds and take in the many shades of green. It is a reminder of how different the natural landscapes can be on a single Galápagos island.

Mamey marks both the beginning and the end of the hiking portion of the route to Colombia's Lost City. Travellers reach the village by vehicle before continuing along the river towards forest camps. The village connects the road journey with the trails that must be followed on foot.

The trail from Mamey passes natural pools, ascents and river scenery. When hikers return, the multi-day trek comes to an end here, leaving time to rest before the drive back towards the coast. For travellers, the village's importance lies in this transition between inhabited places and the mountain trail leading to the archaeological complex.

After the boat crossing on the Guayabero River, the route climbs a forest trail. At El Mirador, the landscape opens up at once: the river bends below, plains stretch towards the horizon, and the green slopes of the Sierra de la Macarena rise on the other side.

This natural lookout is on the El Mirador–Cristalitos trail in the El Billar area near La Macarena. It overlooks the Guayabero's course and the surroundings of the town. After the ascent, it is a pleasant place to stop, take panoramic photographs and see how forest meets savanna.

The trail then continues to Caño Cristalitos. On the Ada Tours itinerary, the viewpoint and stream form a single hiking route with boat sections. Access and the order of visits depend on conservation authority regulations.

Coffee grows in the shade of trees on the slopes near Salento. El Ocaso Farm traces its story from the very beginning: from the coffee plant and hand-picking of cherries to processing, roasting and a freshly prepared cup. Here, it is easy to connect the flavour of coffee with the place where it was grown.

El Ocaso is in the department of Quindío, part of Colombia's coffee region. The property has coffee plantations, gardens and an old house with colonial architecture. Green mountain slopes and paths around the farm add to the experience of learning about production.

On the Ada Tours programme, a local expert leads the visit: you will see the main stages of bean processing and taste both coffee and coffee lemonade. The farm fits well into a day that also includes the Cocora Valley and a walk around Salento. The exact format of the visit depends on the chosen itinerary.
